(CNN) -- President Obama said Tuesday that the country already is "seeing shovels hit the ground" on the first infrastructure repair project funded through the Transportation Department's share of the $787 billion stimulus bill. Workers mark where repairs are needed on Maryland Route 650. Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said, "The work begins today in Montgomery County, Maryland, where a work crew is starting on a project to resurface Maryland State Highway 650 -- a very busy road that has not been fully repaired in 17 years." The resurfacing contract is going to a Pennsylvania-based family-owned company, American Infrastructure, LaHood said. He said the project will support 60 jobs. "And that's how we're going to get the country back on its feet," LaHood added. Mark Compton, director of government affairs for American Infrastructure, said his company received $2.1 million in federal funds, by way of the Maryland State Highway Administration. The money will be used to repave and add safety features to a stretch of the highway. Compton said the cash infusion is the "catalyst" to create 60 jobs, including bringing back some laid-off employees. He said he hopes the workers can be retained beyond this six-month project. "We'll continue to bid, so the goal is to get more projects to keep those guys working, so they can roll off that project onto another," Compton said. CNNMoney: Stimulus funds hit the street . Obama and LaHood on Tuesday announced the release of $27 billion in funds from the stimulus package "to help states create a 21st-century infrastructure." The president said it is part of the "largest new investment in America's infrastructure since President Eisenhower built the Interstate Highway System." Obama said another 200 construction projects would be launched over the next few weeks, "fueling growth in an industry that's been hard hit by our economic crisis." Two weeks ago, Obama signed into law his stimulus plan, known as the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act. The president has said the plan will create or save up to 3.5 million jobs over the next two years. Four-hundred thousand of those will be infrastructure jobs that include rebuilding roads, bridges and schools. LaHood has asked the nation's governors to certify projects and provide assurances that funds from the act will be spent for appropriate infrastructure projects. Obama said transportation projects would be stamped with a special emblem so people can see where their tax dollars are going. Obama said the investments in highways would create or save 150,000 jobs by the end of 2010. The number of jobs being created or saved in one year is more than the number of jobs the Big Three automakers have lost in manufacturing over the past three years, Obama said. By investing in roads "that should have been rebuilt long ago," Obama said, "we can save some 14,000 men and women who lose their lives each year due to bad roads and driving conditions." "Poor roads are a public hazard, and we have a responsibility to fix them," he said.  Watch Obama explain how the roads will save lives » . Obama also announced Tuesday that the Treasury Department and Federal Reserve were launching the Consumer and Business Lending Initiative. When fully implemented, Obama said, the initiative "will generate up to a trillion dollars in new lending for the American people, and this will help unlock our frozen credit markets, which is absolutely essential for economic recovery." CNNMoney's Aaron Smith contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — President Obama said Tuesday that the country is already “seeing shovels hit the ground” on the first infrastructure repair project funded through the Transportation Department’s portion of the $787 billion stimulus bill.

Workers have begun marking areas in need of repair on Maryland Route 650.

Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said, “The work begins today in Montgomery County, Maryland, where a work crew is starting on a project to resurface Maryland State Highway 650 — a very busy road that has not been fully repaired in 17 years.”

LaHood said the resurfacing contract has been awarded to American Infrastructure, a Pennsylvania-based, family-owned company. He added that the project will support 60 jobs.

“And that’s how we’re going to get the country back on its feet,” LaHood said.

Mark Compton, director of government affairs for American Infrastructure, said his company received $2.1 million in federal funds through the Maryland State Highway Administration. The money will be used to repave a stretch of the highway and add safety features.

Compton described the cash infusion as the “catalyst” for creating 60 jobs, including rehiring some laid-off employees. He said he hopes the workers can be retained beyond the six-month project.

“We’ll continue to bid, so the goal is to get more projects to keep those guys working, so they can roll off that project onto another,” Compton said.

Obama and LaHood on Tuesday announced the release of $27 billion in stimulus funds “to help states create a 21st-century infrastructure.” The president said the funding is part of the “largest new investment in America’s infrastructure since President Eisenhower built the Interstate Highway System.”

Obama said another 200 construction projects would be launched over the next few weeks, “fueling growth in an industry that’s been hard hit by our economic crisis.”

Two weeks ago, Obama signed into law his stimulus plan, known as the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act. The president has said the plan will create or save up to 3.5 million jobs over the next two years. Of those, 400,000 will be infrastructure jobs, including positions tied to rebuilding roads, bridges and schools.

LaHood has asked the nation’s governors to certify projects and provide assurances that funds from the act will be spent on appropriate infrastructure projects. Obama said transportation projects would bear a special emblem so people can see where their tax dollars are going.

Obama said investments in highways would create or save 150,000 jobs by the end of 2010. He said the number of jobs created or saved in one year exceeds the number of manufacturing jobs the Big Three automakers have lost over the past three years.

By investing in roads “that should have been rebuilt long ago,” Obama said, “we can save some 14,000 men and women who lose their lives each year due to bad roads and driving conditions.”

“Poor roads are a public hazard, and we have a responsibility to fix them,” he said.

Obama also announced Tuesday that the Treasury Department and Federal Reserve were launching the Consumer and Business Lending Initiative. Once fully implemented, Obama said, the initiative “will generate up to a trillion dollars in new lending for the American people, and this will help unlock our frozen credit markets, which is absolutely essential for economic recovery.”

CNNMoney’s Aaron Smith contributed to this report.

(CNN) — President Obama said Tuesday that the nation is already “seeing shovels hit the ground” as work begins on the first infrastructure repair effort financed by the Transportation Department’s portion of the $787 billion stimulus package.

Crews were marking areas in need of repair along Maryland Route 650.

Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said the project was starting that day in Montgomery County, Maryland, where workers were beginning to resurface Maryland State Highway 650, a heavily traveled road that had not undergone a complete repair in 17 years.

According to LaHood, the resurfacing contract was awarded to American Infrastructure, a family-owned company based in Pennsylvania. He said the work would support 60 jobs.

“That’s how we’re going to get the country back on its feet,” LaHood said.

Mark Compton, American Infrastructure’s director of government affairs, said the company had received $2.1 million in federal funding through the Maryland State Highway Administration. The funds will pay for repaving part of the highway and adding safety improvements.

Compton described the funding as the “catalyst” for creating 60 jobs, including rehiring some workers who had been laid off. He said he hoped the company would be able to keep those employees after the six-month project ends.

“We’ll continue to bid, so the goal is to get more projects to keep those guys working, so they can roll off that project onto another,” Compton said.

CNNMoney: Stimulus funds hit the street.

On Tuesday, Obama and LaHood also announced the release of $27 billion from the stimulus law to “help states create a 21st-century infrastructure.”

Obama said the funding represents part of the “largest new investment in America’s infrastructure since President Eisenhower built the Interstate Highway System.”

The president said roughly 200 additional construction projects would begin in the coming weeks, helping drive growth in an industry that has suffered during the economic downturn.

Two weeks earlier, Obama signed his stimulus measure, formally called the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act, into law. He has said the program will create or preserve as many as 3.5 million jobs over two years. Of those, 400,000 are expected to be infrastructure-related positions involving work such as rebuilding roads, bridges and schools.

LaHood has called on governors across the country to certify projects and guarantee that money from the act will be used for proper infrastructure work.

Obama said transportation projects funded by the law would carry a special symbol so the public could see where tax money is being spent.

The president said highway investments would create or save 150,000 jobs by the end of 2010. He added that the number of jobs created or preserved in a single year would exceed the number of manufacturing jobs lost by the Big Three automakers over the previous three years.

Obama also said that by funding roads “that should have been rebuilt long ago,” the country could save about 14,000 people who die each year because of dangerous roads and driving conditions.

“Poor roads are a public hazard, and we have a responsibility to fix them,” he said.

Watch Obama explain how the roads will save lives »

Obama further announced Tuesday that the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve were beginning the Consumer and Business Lending Initiative. Once fully in place, he said, the program “will generate up to a trillion dollars in new lending for the American people,” helping to thaw frozen credit markets, which he called essential to economic recovery.

CNNMoney’s Aaron Smith contributed to this report.

**Obama announces first transportation project funded by stimulus bill**

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style)** — President Barack Obama on Tuesday announced the first transportation infrastructure project to be funded by the $787 billion economic stimulus package, pointing to a Maryland road improvement effort as an early example of how the administration says the law will put Americans back to work.

The project will repair and resurface a stretch of **Maryland Route 650**, also known as New Hampshire Avenue, a heavily traveled commuter route in the Washington suburbs. Administration officials said the work is intended to improve safety, ease congestion and demonstrate how quickly federal stimulus dollars can move into local projects.

Standing with Transportation Secretary **Ray LaHood**, Obama said the investment marks the beginning of a broader push to rebuild roads, bridges and transit systems while creating jobs during the economic downturn.

“This is the first of many projects that will be getting under way across the country,” Obama said, emphasizing that the stimulus plan is designed to “save or create” millions of jobs by funding projects that are ready to begin quickly.

LaHood said transportation agencies nationwide have been preparing lists of “shovel-ready” projects that can receive federal money and begin construction in the coming weeks and months. The Department of Transportation is overseeing tens of billions of dollars in stimulus funding for highways, bridges, rail and public transit.

The Maryland Route 650 project is expected to support construction and related jobs, including workers involved in paving, engineering, materials supply and traffic management. White House officials have argued that infrastructure spending has a ripple effect, helping not only construction crews but also suppliers, equipment companies and local businesses.

Obama also used the announcement to highlight a separate effort to loosen frozen credit markets. The administration said it is moving forward with a new lending initiative aimed at increasing the availability of loans for consumers and small businesses. The program is intended to help revive lending for auto loans, student loans, credit cards and business financing — areas that tightened sharply during the financial crisis.

The president said infrastructure investment and expanded lending are part of the same economic recovery strategy: creating jobs immediately while restoring confidence in the broader economy.

Republicans have criticized the stimulus bill as too expensive and questioned whether the money will be spent efficiently. Obama and his advisers have said the spending will be tracked closely and that the public will be able to monitor projects funded by the package.

“This plan is not just about putting people to work today,” Obama said. “It’s about laying the foundation for long-term economic growth.”

**Obama Administration Releases Stimulus Funds for Road Repairs, Including Maryland Route 650 Resurfacing**

**By Staff Reporter**

**WASHINGTON/MARYLAND —** The Obama administration has begun releasing federal stimulus funds for transportation projects across the country, including money for resurfacing work on Maryland State Highway 650, as part of a broader effort to jump-start the economy, create jobs and address long-deferred infrastructure repairs.

Maryland State Highway 650, better known for much of its route as New Hampshire Avenue, is among the roadways slated for improvement under funding made available through the federal economic recovery package. The resurfacing project is intended to repair worn pavement, improve driving conditions and extend the life of the busy commuter corridor, which connects communities in the Washington suburbs and carries significant local and regional traffic.

The funding comes from the Obama administration’s economic stimulus program, formally known as the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, which was designed to counter the recession by pushing federal dollars into “shovel-ready” projects. Transportation improvements were a major part of the plan, with road, bridge and transit investments promoted as a way to put construction crews to work quickly while improving public infrastructure.

Administration officials have argued that road repair projects are especially well suited to the recovery effort because they can begin relatively quickly, rely on existing engineering plans and employ workers in construction, paving, materials production and related industries. State and local governments, facing budget shortfalls during the downturn, have looked to the federal funds to keep projects moving that might otherwise have been delayed.

In Maryland, resurfacing Route 650 is expected to include pavement milling, asphalt overlay and related safety improvements such as fresh lane markings. While resurfacing does not typically involve major road widening or reconstruction, transportation officials say it can produce immediate benefits for motorists by reducing rough pavement, potholes and vehicle wear.

The project also fits into a larger national strategy. The Obama administration’s recovery plan sought to combine short-term economic stimulus with long-term investment in infrastructure, energy, education and public services. Road repairs were among the most visible components of the program, with signs appearing at work zones around the country identifying projects funded by the federal recovery act.

Supporters of the stimulus package said projects like the Maryland Route 650 resurfacing demonstrated how federal spending could directly support local jobs while improving essential public assets. Contractors, equipment operators, laborers, asphalt suppliers and trucking companies were expected to benefit from the flow of transportation dollars.

Critics, however, questioned whether infrastructure spending could move quickly enough to provide immediate economic relief and raised concerns about the size of federal spending and its impact on the deficit. Some also argued that resurfacing and maintenance projects, while useful, did not always represent the kind of transformative infrastructure investment the country needed.

State transportation agencies receiving stimulus funds were required to meet federal reporting and accountability standards, including tracking project costs, work progress and job impacts. The administration emphasized transparency as a central feature of the recovery program, seeking to reassure taxpayers that money was being directed to eligible projects and used promptly.

For Maryland commuters, the practical effect of the Route 650 project would be more immediate: smoother pavement, improved lane visibility and fewer maintenance-related hazards along a heavily used state highway. Temporary lane closures and construction delays were expected during the resurfacing work, though such projects are often scheduled during off-peak hours to reduce disruption.

The release of funds for Route 650 is one piece of a much larger transportation push under the recovery plan. Across the nation, similar projects were launched to repair highways, rehabilitate bridges, upgrade transit systems and support local transportation networks. The administration presented the effort as both an emergency response to the economic crisis and a down payment on rebuilding the country’s infrastructure.

As work begins on Maryland State Highway 650 and other federally supported projects, the success of the stimulus program will be measured not only by miles of pavement repaired, but also by whether the investments help stabilize employment, support local economies and restore public confidence during a period of deep economic uncertainty.

**Obama: Stimulus-Funded Road Work Is Under Way**

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style news article, 2009)** — President Obama said Wednesday that money from the $787 billion economic stimulus package is beginning to move from Washington into local construction projects, as the administration sought to show Americans visible signs that the recovery plan is creating jobs.

Speaking as transportation projects broke ground around the country, Obama said the work marked “the beginning of a new wave of investment” in roads, bridges and transit systems that have long needed repair.

“This is about putting Americans back to work,” Obama said. “It is about rebuilding the roads and bridges that our families and businesses depend on every day, and it is about making sure that taxpayer dollars are spent quickly, wisely and transparently.”

The administration has been under pressure to demonstrate that the stimulus plan, signed into law in February, is having an immediate effect on an economy battered by recession, rising unemployment and tight credit. White House officials said thousands of transportation projects have been approved or are moving toward construction, with states receiving federal funds for work ranging from highway resurfacing to bridge repair.

Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said the department is working closely with governors and state transportation agencies to move projects forward while monitoring spending.

“We are getting money out the door, but we are also making sure there is accountability,” LaHood said. “These are projects that can create jobs now and leave communities with better infrastructure for years to come.”

Republicans have criticized the stimulus package as too expensive and too slow to affect the economy, arguing that tax relief and spending restraint would do more to spur growth. Administration officials counter that large-scale public works projects take time to organize but will support construction jobs and related industries as the year progresses.

For contractors, the new funding is arriving at a critical moment. Many construction firms have seen private-sector work disappear as businesses delay expansion and local governments struggle with declining tax revenue.

“We had crews sitting idle and equipment parked,” said Mike Reynolds, a highway contractor whose company is preparing to begin a resurfacing project funded in part by the stimulus. “This gives us a chance to bring people back, buy materials and keep the company moving.”

Obama said the projects are part of a broader effort to stabilize the economy, which includes aid to states, tax cuts for workers and investments in energy, education and health care technology.

“There is no single project or single program that will solve this crisis overnight,” the president said. “But every road repaired, every bridge strengthened and every worker rehired is a step toward recovery.”

White House officials said the public will be able to track stimulus spending through federal reporting requirements and online updates, a transparency effort intended to prevent waste and reassure taxpayers.

The president acknowledged that the road to recovery would be difficult, but said the start of infrastructure work shows the recovery plan is moving from legislation to action.

“Today, the work begins,” Obama said. “And with it, so does the work of rebuilding America’s economy.”

**WASHINGTON (CNN) --** The Obama administration Tuesday marked the start of the first highway construction project funded by the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, while announcing the release of nearly **$27 billion in Transportation Department funds** intended to jump-start road and bridge work across the country.

The first project, a highway resurfacing effort in Maryland, is being touted by the White House as an early sign that money from the $787 billion economic stimulus package is beginning to reach local communities. Administration officials said the project is part of a broader push to repair aging infrastructure while putting Americans back to work during the recession.

Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said the release of the federal highway funds would allow states to move quickly on “shovel-ready” projects, including road repairs, bridge rehabilitation and transit improvements.

The administration said transportation spending under the recovery act is expected to **save or create tens of thousands of jobs**, with broader stimulus efforts aimed at supporting or creating about **3.5 million jobs** nationwide. Officials said highway projects would support construction workers, engineers, suppliers and other businesses tied to infrastructure development.

President Obama has argued that infrastructure spending is one of the fastest ways to inject money into the economy while addressing long-delayed public works needs.

“This is about jobs now and a stronger economy later,” the administration said in promoting the funding release.

The highway announcement came as the administration also moved to address the nation’s frozen credit markets. Treasury officials outlined the **Consumer and Business Lending Initiative**, a program designed to encourage lending to households and businesses by supporting markets for loans such as auto loans, student loans, credit card debt and small-business financing.

The lending initiative, working with the Federal Reserve’s Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility, is intended to help revive the flow of credit by backing securities tied to consumer and business loans. Officials said restoring lending is critical to stabilizing the economy, because families and companies have struggled to borrow money during the financial crisis.

Republicans have criticized the stimulus package as too costly and questioned whether the spending will create jobs quickly enough. The White House has countered that the recession requires aggressive action and that infrastructure projects provide both immediate employment and long-term economic benefits.

States are required to obligate a portion of the transportation money quickly or risk losing it to states that can move faster. Administration officials said that requirement is meant to ensure that stimulus dollars are spent rapidly and transparently.

The Transportation Department said additional highway and transit projects are expected to begin in the coming weeks as states finalize contracts and submit plans for federal approval.

**BREAKING NEWS: Obama Says “Shovels Hit the Ground” as Stimulus Infrastructure Projects Begin**

**WASHINGTON —** President Barack Obama announced today that the first wave of infrastructure projects funded by the federal economic stimulus package is moving from planning to construction, declaring that “shovels hit the ground” as the administration seeks to turn billions in recovery spending into jobs, safer roads, and visible improvements across the country.

Speaking as his administration accelerates implementation of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, Obama highlighted transportation and public-works projects as a central part of the effort to revive the economy. The president said the goal is not only to create and preserve jobs, but also to invest in long-delayed infrastructure needs — including road repairs, bridge work, and safety improvements.

Among the projects cited was work in **Montgomery County**, where officials are moving forward with infrastructure improvements expected to receive stimulus support. The administration has pointed to such local projects as examples of how federal dollars can be quickly translated into construction activity, contractor hiring, and economic activity in surrounding communities.

Obama emphasized that transportation spending will focus heavily on **road safety**, with projects aimed at repairing deteriorating pavement, upgrading intersections, improving signage and traffic flow, and addressing hazards that have built up after years of deferred maintenance. Administration officials said these types of projects are often “shovel-ready” because planning and engineering work has already been completed, allowing construction to begin quickly once funds are released.

The president also underscored the role of **governors in certifying stimulus projects**, a requirement intended to ensure that federal funds are directed toward legitimate, ready-to-go investments that serve a public purpose. Governors must certify that projects have been properly reviewed and that the spending is an appropriate use of recovery money. The certification process is designed to provide accountability while still moving funds into the economy at a rapid pace.

The announcement comes as the White House faces pressure to show tangible results from the massive stimulus law, which was passed in response to the deepening recession and financial crisis. Obama said infrastructure spending is one of the clearest ways to demonstrate the recovery plan in action, because residents will be able to see crews at work, roads being repaired, and public facilities improved.

The administration has repeatedly described the country’s aging infrastructure as both an economic weakness and an opportunity. Groups such as **American Infrastructure** and other construction and engineering firms are expected to compete for or carry out some of the federally supported work, depending on state and local contracting decisions. The White House says the broader aim is to help businesses retain workers, bring back laid-off employees, and support industries tied to construction, materials, transportation, and equipment.

At the same time, Obama and his economic team are pairing infrastructure spending with wider financial-stabilization measures. The administration pointed to ongoing **Treasury Department and Federal Reserve lending efforts** aimed at easing credit conditions, supporting consumer and business lending, and restoring confidence in financial markets. Those initiatives are intended to complement stimulus spending by making it easier for companies, municipalities, and households to access financing during the downturn.

Officials said the Treasury and Fed efforts remain critical because public-works spending alone cannot repair the damage caused by frozen credit markets and the collapse in private investment. By combining direct federal spending with lending programs, the administration hopes to restart both public and private economic activity.

Obama argued that the infrastructure push will deliver immediate and long-term benefits: paychecks for workers now, safer and more efficient roads for commuters, and stronger foundations for future growth. But he also acknowledged the need for oversight, saying the administration will track projects closely to reduce waste and ensure that recovery dollars are spent effectively.

The president’s message was clear: the stimulus is no longer just legislation on paper. With governors certifying projects, local governments preparing contracts, companies mobilizing crews, and federal agencies coordinating funding, the administration says the recovery effort is entering a more visible phase — one marked by construction signs, work zones, and, in Obama’s words, “shovels” finally hitting “the ground.”
